lead: A continuous signal can be replaced by a list of numbers if it has no frequency above fmax and we sample faster than 2fmax. The samples then keep all the information, and an ideal low-pass filter turns them back into the smooth waveform. This is the bridge from continuous-time to discrete-time processing: phone audio, ECG recorders and digital controllers all store samples instead of a continuous voltage. Sampling too slowly loses information for good; that failure is the next chapter, aliasing and anti-aliasing filters.
prereq: You need: the Fourier transform, the sinc spectrum and ideal filters (see Fourier series and Fourier transform); the impulse and standard signals (see Classification of signals and systems).

sections.h3: The sampling theorem and its numbers

blocks.text: A signal is band-limited when its Fourier transform X(f) is zero for |f| > fmax, where fmax is the highest frequency in hertz. Sampling takes its values at the instants t = nTs, where n = …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, … is any integer and Ts is the sampling interval in seconds. The sampling rate is fs = 1/Ts samples per second, written in hertz.

Sampling theorem. A signal band-limited to fmax is completely determined by its samples x(nTs) if fs > 2fmax. The rate 2fmax is the Nyquist rate, a property of the signal. The longest allowed spacing, 1/(2fmax), is the Nyquist interval. Half the sampling rate, fs/2, is the Nyquist frequency, a property of the sampler: components below it are kept as they are, and a component above it folds onto a lower frequency.
Here f<sub>s</sub> is the sampling rate in Hz, T<sub>s</sub> the sampling interval in s and f<sub>max</sub> the highest frequency in the signal in Hz.

The inequality is strict. At f<sub>s</sub> = 2f<sub>max</sub>, a cosine exactly at f<sub>max</sub> is sampled twice per period at the same two phases. Sampled at its peaks it looks fine, but sampled at its zero crossings every sample is 0, so its amplitude and phase cannot be recovered. Some syllabi call the result the Nyquist–Shannon or Whittaker–Kotelnikov–Shannon theorem.

sections.h3: Impulse-train model and the repeated spectrum

blocks.text: To see why the theorem holds, model the sampler as multiplication by an impulse train p(t) = Σ δ(t − nT<sub>s</sub>), the sum running over all integers n. Each impulse in the product carries one sample value as its area.
Here x<sub>s</sub>(t) is the impulse-sampled signal and x(nT<sub>s</sub>) the sample at t = nT<sub>s</sub>.

The Fourier transform of the impulse train is another impulse train, of strength 1/T<sub>s</sub> at every multiple of f<sub>s</sub>. Multiplication in time becomes convolution in frequency, and convolving X(f) with an impulse at kf<sub>s</sub> simply shifts it there. So the spectrum of the samples is the original spectrum repeated every f<sub>s</sub> hertz:
Here X<sub>s</sub>(f) is the spectrum of the samples, X(f) the original spectrum, and k runs over all integers. Every copy is scaled by 1/T<sub>s</sub> = f<sub>s</sub>.

The copy at k = 0 is the baseband copy; it runs from −fmax to fmax. The next copy starts at fs − fmax. The copies stay apart when fs − fmax > fmax, which is exactly fs > 2fmax. The empty gap between them, from fmax to fs − fmax, is the guard band, of width fs − 2fmax. If the copies overlap, high frequencies land on low ones: that is aliasing, the subject of aliasing and anti-aliasing filters.

An ideal low-pass filter with cutoff f<sub>s</sub>/2 and passband gain T<sub>s</sub> keeps the baseband copy and removes all the others. The gain T<sub>s</sub> cancels the 1/T<sub>s</sub> scaling, so the output is x(t) with its original amplitude. Any cutoff inside the guard band works; f<sub>s</sub>/2 is the usual choice because it sits in the middle.
Here H(f) is the frequency response of the reconstruction filter.

In time, this filter's impulse response is h(t) = sinc(t/Ts), the inverse transform of a rectangle of height Ts and width fs. Passing the impulse train through it replaces each impulse by a sinc pulse of height x(nTs) centred at nTs. Adding the pulses gives the interpolation formula:
Here sinc(u) = sin(πu)/(πu) with sinc(0) = 1, and the sum runs over all integers n.

Each sinc is 1 at its own sampling instant and 0 at every other sampling instant, so at t = nTs the sum returns exactly the sample x(nTs); between instants the pulses fill in the smooth curve. This filter is ideal: it is non-causal and has a vertical edge. Real circuits hold each sample and then smooth the staircase, which droops at high frequencies; that practical side and the band-pass case are in low-pass, band-pass and practical sampling.

examples.question: A voltage x(t) = 3 cos(2π·200t) + 2 cos(2π·450t) volts is sampled at f<sub>s</sub> = 1000 Hz. Find f<sub>max</sub>, the Nyquist rate, the Nyquist interval, T<sub>s</sub> and the reconstruction filter. List the spectral lines between 0 and 1500 Hz, and find the guard band.
steps: The frequency of each cosine is the number multiplying t inside 2π(…): 200 Hz and 450 Hz. So f<sub>max</sub> = 450 Hz.
Nyquist rate = 2f<sub>max</sub> = 2 × 450 = 900 Hz. Nyquist interval = 1/900 s ≈ 1.11 ms. Since 1000 Hz > 900 Hz, the condition f<sub>s</sub> > 2f<sub>max</sub> holds.
Reconstruction filter: ideal low-pass, cutoff f<sub>s</sub>/2 = 500 Hz, passband gain T<sub>s</sub> = 0.001.
Spectral lines on the positive axis: baseband at 200 and 450 Hz; the copy at 1000 Hz gives 1000 − 450 = 550, 1000 − 200 = 800, 1000 + 200 = 1200 and 1000 + 450 = 1450 Hz.
Guard band: from f<sub>max</sub> = 450 Hz up to the lowest copy line 550 Hz, width 550 − 450 = 100 Hz = f<sub>s</sub> − 2f<sub>max</sub>. The 500 Hz cutoff sits in the middle of it.
The filter passes 200 and 450 Hz and stops 550 Hz and above, so the output is the original x(t).
examples.answer: f<sub>max</sub> = 450 Hz, Nyquist rate = 900 Hz, Nyquist interval ≈ 1.11 ms, T<sub>s</sub> = 1 ms, filter cutoff 500 Hz with gain 0.001, copy lines at 550, 800, 1200 and 1450 Hz, guard band 100 Hz; sampling at 1000 Hz is safe.

traps: Nyquist rate (2f<sub>max</sub>, fixed by the signal) and Nyquist frequency (f<sub>s</sub>/2, fixed by the sampler) are different ideas. They are equal only when f<sub>s</sub> = 2f<sub>max</sub>, the borderline case.
Dropping the gain T<sub>s</sub> of the reconstruction filter: the output is then scaled by 1/T<sub>s</sub>.
Writing f<sub>s</sub> ≥ 2f<sub>max</sub>. A sinusoid exactly at f<sub>max</sub> is not safe at f<sub>s</sub> = 2f<sub>max</sub>; the condition is strict.
Unit slips: T<sub>s</sub> in seconds, f<sub>s</sub> in hertz; 1 ms = 0.001 s, and 1/(1 kHz) = 1 ms, not 1 s.
Guard band is f<sub>s</sub> − 2f<sub>max</sub>, the gap between the top of the baseband and the bottom of the first copy, not f<sub>s</sub> − f<sub>max</sub>.

quiz.q: Define Nyquist rate and Nyquist frequency.
quiz.a: Nyquist rate is the minimum sampling rate 2f<sub>max</sub> for a signal band-limited to f<sub>max</sub>. Nyquist frequency is half the sampling rate, f<sub>s</sub>/2. For f<sub>max</sub> = 450 Hz and f<sub>s</sub> = 1000 Hz they are 900 Hz and 500 Hz.

quiz.q: Why is f<sub>s</sub> > 2f<sub>max</sub> written with a strict inequality?
quiz.a: At f<sub>s</sub> = 2f<sub>max</sub> a cosine at f<sub>max</sub> is sampled at the same two phases every period. If those are its zero crossings, every sample is 0, so amplitude and phase are lost.

quiz.q: x(t) = 5 cos(2π·300t) is sampled at 800 Hz. Is it safe? Give T<sub>s</sub>, the filter cutoff and the guard band.
quiz.a: f<sub>max</sub> = 300 Hz, Nyquist rate 600 Hz, and 800 > 600, so it is safe. T<sub>s</sub> = 1/800 = 1.25 ms; cutoff f<sub>s</sub>/2 = 400 Hz; guard band = 800 − 600 = 200 Hz (from 300 to 500 Hz).

quiz.q: A 450 Hz component is sampled at 1200 Hz. Find the lowest copy line and the guard band.
quiz.a: The first copy line is 1200 − 450 = 750 Hz. Guard band = 750 − 450 = 300 Hz = f<sub>s</sub> − 2f<sub>max</sub>.

quiz.q: What do the cutoff and the gain of the ideal reconstruction filter each do?
quiz.a: The cutoff f<sub>s</sub>/2 keeps the baseband copy and removes the copies centred at ±f<sub>s</sub>, ±2f<sub>s</sub>, …. The gain T<sub>s</sub> cancels the 1/T<sub>s</sub> scaling that sampling put on every copy.

quiz.q: Write the interpolation formula and say what each sinc pulse does at the sampling instants.
quiz.a: x(t) = Σ x(nT<sub>s</sub>) sinc((t − nT<sub>s</sub>)/T<sub>s</sub>). Each pulse is 1 at its own instant nT<sub>s</sub> and 0 at every other sampling instant.

quiz.q: A signal has 200 Hz and 450 Hz components and is sampled at 900 Hz. Is exact reconstruction guaranteed?
quiz.a: No. The Nyquist rate is 900 Hz and the condition is strict. The 450 Hz component sits exactly at f<sub>s</sub>/2, where its samples depend on its phase, so its amplitude and phase cannot be recovered in general.

beyond: Audio codecs and software-defined radios choose f<sub>s</sub> from the band of interest and use steep digital filters when they lower the rate. Medical recorders and vibration monitors use the same theorem to set their sampling rates. Compressive sensing samples fewer values when a signal is sparse, and sigma-delta converters sample very fast at low resolution and filter digitally. Search next: sinc interpolation, oversampling, compressive sensing.
